messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bao, at sixty-nine, had believed the most difficult parts of his life were behind him. After his wife passed, his work as a nanny for a young family provided a gentle rhythm to his days, a way to fill the quiet house with the sounds of life. That was before his youngest daughter, Linh, was rushed to the hospital with a fever that spiraled into a terrifying, week-long battle in the intensive care unit. Though Linh made a full recovery nearly a year ago, the man who sat in the clinic waiting room was not the same one who had walked into that hospital. He was, in his own words, someone he no longer recognized.

The trauma did not live in him as a coherent story. He found he could not tell a clear narrative of what happened, not even to himself. Instead, it existed as a series of sensory ambushes, more vivid and real than his memory of breakfast that morning. It was the high-pitched, rhythmic beep of the machines, the acrid smell of antiseptic, and the sight of Linh’s small body overwhelmed by tubes and wires. These were not memories of the past; when they came, it felt like it was happening right now, the panic and helplessness as fresh and sharp as they were in that sterile, windowless room. The sheer, agonizing vividness of these moments drove him to do anything to keep them at bay. At work, if the toddler he cared for developed even a slight cough, Bao would immediately launch into a loud, distracting game or turn on cartoons, his mind racing to build a wall against the intrusive images he knew were waiting to flood in.

This constant, frantic effort to suppress his thoughts and distract himself only seemed to keep the memories fragmented and potent. Because he never let himself assemble the pieces into a whole story with a beginning, middle, and an end where his daughter survived, the fragments retained their full power. His refusal to think about the trauma ensured it never became a part of his past, but remained a perpetual, threatening present. This cycle of unprocessed memory reinforced his deepest fears about himself. Each time a flashback broke through his defenses, it served as fresh evidence that he had been permanently changed for the worse. The calm, capable father he had once been was gone, replaced by this frightened stranger who couldn't even handle a common cold.

These beliefs about his own irreparable damage dictated his every move. Believing he was fundamentally broken, the idea of seeking medical or psychological help felt pointless. He had also developed a profound distrust of others since the ordeal; he couldn’t shake the memory of the doctors’ calm, placid faces as they delivered terrifying news, and he was now certain that people were not what they seemed. This conviction made him avoid his own doctor and isolate himself from friends who tried to ask how he was doing. Instead, his strategy was internal: to keep his mind occupied at all times. The silence in his apartment after work was unbearable, a vacuum that would immediately fill with the sounds of the ICU. He kept the television on from the moment he woke until he fell into a fitful sleep, the noise a necessary shield.

The feedback loop was now a prison. The fragmented, present-tense memories confirmed his belief that he was permanently damaged, and this belief fueled his avoidance and thought suppression. In turn, these strategies prevented the memory from ever being integrated, leaving it as a collection of raw, terrifying moments ready to strike again. His conviction that he was an unrecognizable version of his former self would even color the memories themselves, foregrounding his own helplessness and terror. He felt he had failed a fundamental test, and the memory was his constant, shameful reminder. He was brought to therapy not by his own choice, but by Linh’s gentle insistence. She had noticed his extreme reactions to her slightest sniffle, his constant, humming tension, and the way he looked right through her sometimes. Bao came to his first session exhausted and deeply skeptical, terrified that confirming his fear—that he is permanently broken—is all that can happen here.
